title: Nessus. Herculis mors
titleEn: The Death of Hercules on Oeta — Metamorphoses IX.172–272
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Hercules is burning alive from a gift he cannot tear off his body, and the tale gives him first a speech: a curse flung at Juno, then the whole catalogue of his labours, set out as a charge against a goddess who has worn herself out giving orders while he is not worn out obeying them. He catches sight of Lichas, whom he charges with bringing the gift, and hurls him into the sea, where he hardens in mid-air into a low rock that sailors still will not tread on. Then he has trees felled on Oeta and built into a pyre, spreads the lion-skin over the top of it and lies back with his neck on his club, with no more concern on his face than a guest at a dinner. Jupiter tells the frightened gods that only the half of his son that came from his mother can burn; the fire takes away every recognisable likeness of him, and what is left, drawn from Jupiter, is carried up in a four-horse chariot to the stars.

sentences.t:
Nec modus est: sorbent avidae praecordia flammae,
caeruleusque fluit toto de corpore sudor,
ambustique sonant nervi:
sentences.l: And there is no limit: greedy flames drink down his vitals, and a livid sweat flows from his whole body, and his burnt sinews crackle:
sentences.i: There is no end to it: the flames drink his vitals down greedily, a dark sweat runs from his whole body, his scorched sinews crackle aloud:
sentences.n: praecordia are the parts about the heart, the vitals — the midriff and what it holds, not the chest as a whole. sorbent is the verb for sucking or swallowing a liquid down, so the flames drink him. caeruleus covers dark blue and the livid blue-black of a bruise; the sweat is not the colour a body's sweat should be. The present tense here (sorbent, fluit, sonant) puts the agony in front of the reader as it happens.

sentences.t:
caecaque medullis
tabe liquefactis tollens ad sidera palmas
“cladibus,” exclamat “Saturnia, pascere nostris,
sentences.l: and, with his marrow melted by an unseen wasting, lifting his palms to the stars, he cries out: “On our ruin, Saturn's daughter, feed,
sentences.i: and with his marrow melted away by an unseen corruption, he lifts his palms to the stars and cries out: “Feed on my ruin, daughter of Saturn,
sentences.n: medullis liquefactis is an ablative absolute, “the marrow having been melted”, with caeca tabe (“by an unseen wasting”) as its means; tabes is the word for a rotting or a wasting away. pascere here is not the infinitive but the second-person imperative of pasco in its middle use, “feed yourself, gorge yourself” — the form that looks like an infinitive is the trap. Saturnia, “Saturn's daughter”, is Juno; he will not use her name. nostris is the poetic plural for “my”, which he keeps up through the speech.

sentences.t:
pascere et hanc pestem specta, crudelis, ab alto
corque ferum satia.
sentences.l: feed, and watch this plague from on high, cruel one, and sate your savage heart.
sentences.i: Feed, and from your height look on this plague of mine, cruel goddess, and glut your savage heart.
sentences.n: pascere stands near the close of line 176 and again at the head of line 177: the same imperative twice over across the line-break, so that the demand is made and then made again before anything else is said. specta and satia are two more imperatives in the same run; crudelis is vocative, aimed at her. hanc pestem, “this plague”, is what is destroying him, held up for her to look at.

sentences.t:
Vel si miserandus et hosti,
hoc est, si tibi sum, diris cruciatibus aegram
invisamque animam natamque laboribus aufer:
sentences.l: Or if I am to be pitied even by an enemy — that is, if I am by you — take away this life, sick with dreadful torments and hated and born for labours:
sentences.i: Or if I deserve pity even from an enemy — that is, from you — then take away this life of mine, sick with hideous torments, hated, born for hard labour:
sentences.n: miserandus is a gerundive, “to be pitied”, with hosti as the dative of the person by whom; hoc est, si tibi sum then supplies the sting — he names an enemy first and identifies her as the enemy second. aegram, invisam and natam all agree with animam, three adjectives stacked on the one noun before the imperative aufer finally arrives. laboribus is dative with natam, “born for labours”, and labor is also the standing word for the tasks he is about to list. invisam can be “hated” or “hateful”, and the Latin does not settle whose loathing is meant.

sentences.t: hoc mihi munus erit; decet haec dare dona novercam.
sentences.l: this will be a gift for me; it befits a stepmother to give such gifts.
sentences.i: That would be a gift to me — and gifts like these are exactly what a stepmother should give.
sentences.n: munus and dona are both the language of gift-giving, turned inside out: what he asks for is his own death, and the fitting giver is a stepmother. noverca is the standing figure of malice in Latin, and Juno is literally that to him — his father's wife, not his mother. Magnus prints hoc mihi munus erit, “this will be a gift for me”; some editions print mors, “death will be my gift”, which says outright what hoc only points at.

sentences.t:
Ergo ego foedantem peregrino templa cruore
Busirin domui saevoque alimenta parentis
Antaeo eripui?
sentences.l: Was it I, then, who tamed Busiris, defiling his temples with the blood of strangers, and who tore from savage Antaeus the sustenance of his parent?
sentences.i: Was it I, then, who broke Busiris, who fouled his own temples with the blood of strangers, and who took from savage Antaeus the nourishment his mother gave him?
sentences.n: Ergo ego opens the catalogue of the labours as an indignant question: it is one long list of things done, put as a complaint. domui is the perfect of domo, “I tamed, I subdued”, not a form of domus. Busirin is the accusative of Busiris, keeping its Greek ending; he is the king who cut the throats of foreigners at his own altars, which is what foedantem peregrino templa cruore describes. Antaeo is dative of separation with eripui; alimenta parentis is the earth, his mother, whose touch gave him back his strength — so the way to beat him was to hold him off the ground.

sentences.t:
Nec me pastoris Hiberi
forma triplex, nec forma triplex tua, Cerbere, movit?
sentences.l: Did not the threefold shape of the Iberian herdsman move me, nor your threefold shape, Cerberus?
sentences.i: Did the three-bodied herdsman of Spain not shake me — nor that threefold shape of yours, Cerberus?
sentences.n: The pastor Hiberus, the herdsman of the far west, is Geryon, who had three bodies; Cerberus had three heads. Ovid puts the same two words, forma triplex, on both, so the two lines pair them by their arithmetic. movit is “moved” in the sense of shook or daunted; the literal keeps “move” to show the verb, and being daunted is what it means here. And in the middle of the sentence Hercules turns aside to speak to Cerberus himself — an apostrophe, a device this part uses several times.

sentences.t: Vosne, manus, validi pressistis cornua tauri?
sentences.l: Was it you, hands, that pressed down the horns of the mighty bull?
sentences.i: Was it you, my own hands, that forced down the horns of the great bull?
sentences.n: He now turns from the goddess to his own hands and addresses them: manus is vocative, and the -ne on Vosne makes it a question. From here the labours are credited to them — vestrum, vestrum, vestra in the lines that follow. The bull is the one taken in Crete.

sentences.t:
Vestrum opus Elis habet, vestrum Stymphalides undae
Partheniumque nemus?
sentences.l: Elis holds your work, and the Stymphalian waters your work, and the Parthenian grove?
sentences.i: Is it your work that Elis keeps, and the Stymphalian waters, and the wood of Parthenius?
sentences.n: habet is stated once and understood twice — Latin drops the repeated verb where English wants it back. Each place stands for the labour done there: Elis for the cattle-yards of Augeas, the Stymphalian water for the birds driven off it, the wood of Parthenius for the hind. Naming the place instead of the deed is a metonymy, and it makes the list move faster than a narrative could.

sentences.t:
Vestra virtute relatus
Thermodontiaco caelatus balteus auro
pomaque ab insomni concustodita dracone?
sentences.l: By your valour was brought back the belt engraved with Thermodontian gold, and the apples guarded by the sleepless dragon?
sentences.i: Was it by your strength that the belt chased with the gold of Thermodon was brought back, and the apples the sleepless dragon guarded?
sentences.n: relatus stands without its auxiliary est, which verse leaves out freely. The Thermodon is the Amazons' river, so Thermodontiaco auro means the belt is Amazon work — the girdle taken from their queen. concustodita puts con- in front of custodio to make the guarding closer and harder: kept under watch, not merely watched. insomni, “sleepless”, is why the guard could not be waited out.

sentences.t:
Nec mihi Centauri potuere resistere, nec mi
Arcadiae vastator aper?
sentences.l: And could the Centaurs not stand against me, nor the boar, ravager of Arcadia?
sentences.i: Could the Centaurs not hold out against me — nor the boar that laid Arcadia waste?
sentences.n: potuere is potuerunt, the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere; you will meet it constantly in verse, and twice more in this part. mi in the same line is the shortened form of mihi, and it lets him say the pronoun twice without repeating himself exactly. vastator is an agent noun, “the one who lays waste”, in apposition to aper.

sentences.t:
Nec profuit hydrae
crescere per damnum geminasque resumere vires?
sentences.l: And did it not profit the hydra to grow through loss and to take up twofold strength?
sentences.i: And did it not avail the hydra to grow by its own losses and take back doubled strength?
sentences.n: profuit takes the dative hydrae, and the two infinitives crescere and resumere are its subject: growing and recovering are what did the hydra no good. crescere per damnum, “to grow through loss”, states the paradox of the creature in three words — each head cut off came back as two. geminas is “twin”, so the strength is not just greater but doubled.

sentences.t:
Quid tum? Thracis equos humano sanguine pingues
plenaque corporibus laceris praesepia vidi
visaque deieci dominumque ipsosque peremi.
sentences.l: What then? The Thracian's horses, fat with human blood, and mangers full of mangled bodies I saw, and what I had seen I threw down, and I killed both the master and the horses themselves.
sentences.i: What of that? I saw the Thracian's horses gorged on human blood and the mangers heaped with torn bodies — and having seen them I pulled them down, and killed the master and the horses alike.
sentences.n: Thracis is the genitive of Thrax, “the Thracian”: the man is named by his nation rather than by his name. visa is neuter plural and picks up praesepia, the mangers, and deieci is the verb for pulling a structure to the ground; ipsos then goes back to the horses. Magnus prints Quid tum?, “what then?”, breaking cleanly before the new question; some editions print cum, which would fold the line into “what, when I saw…” instead.

sentences.t:
His elisa iacet moles Nemeaea lacertis,
hac caelum cervice tuli.
sentences.l: By these arms the Nemean mass lies crushed; on this neck I bore up the sky.
sentences.i: It is by these arms that the Nemean bulk lies crushed; it was this neck that held up the sky.
sentences.n: His and hac are demonstratives with a gesture behind them: he is still pointing at his own body, as he was at Vosne, manus. moles Nemeaea, “the Nemean mass”, names the lion by its sheer bulk rather than by its species, and elisa is the participle of elido, to squeeze or crush the life out. tuli is the perfect of fero: he took the weight of the sky on his shoulders when he relieved Atlas of it.

sentences.t:
Defessa iubendo est
saeva Iovis coniunx: ego sum indefessus agendo.
sentences.l: Worn out with commanding is the savage wife of Jupiter: I am unwearied in doing.
sentences.i: Jupiter's savage wife has worn herself out with giving orders; I am not worn out with carrying them out.
sentences.n: The whole point sits in two pairs: defessa against indefessus, and the two ablative gerunds iubendo against agendo. She tires of ordering; he does not tire of doing. He still refuses her name — saeva Iovis coniunx, “the savage wife of Jupiter”, is a way of calling her his father's wife rather than his stepmother.

sentences.t:
Sed nova pestis adest, cui nec virtute resisti
nec telis armisque potest.
sentences.l: But a new plague is at hand, against which it cannot be resisted, neither by valour nor by darts and arms.
sentences.i: But a new plague is upon me, one there is no resisting — not by courage, not by missile or weapon.
sentences.n: resisti potest is an impersonal passive: Latin can say “it is not able to be resisted” with nobody named as the one resisting, which is exactly the helplessness he is describing. resisto takes the dative, so the thing not resisted is cui. pestis picks up hanc pestem from line 177, so the plague he told Juno to look at is now named as a thing no strength answers.

sentences.t:
Pulmonibus errat
ignis edax imis perque omnes pascitur artus.
sentences.l: Through the deepest lungs a devouring fire wanders, and through all my limbs it feeds.
sentences.i: A devouring fire roams in the depths of my lungs and feeds all through my limbs.
sentences.n: imis goes with pulmonibus, “the lowest lungs”, the bottom of the breath. edax, “eating”, is an adjective built straight off edo, and pascitur is the same verb he threw at Juno at 176 and 177: he told her to feed on his ruin, and now the fire is feeding on him. The appetite he wished on the goddess and the appetite that is eating him are named by the one verb.

sentences.t:
At valet Eurystheus!—et sunt qui credere possint
esse deos!”
sentences.l: And yet Eurystheus is in good health! — and there are those who can believe that gods exist!”
sentences.i: And Eurystheus thrives! — and there are men who can believe there are gods!”
sentences.n: valet is the ordinary word for being in good health, and the whole force of the line is that it is spent on Eurystheus, the king who set the labours, while the man who did them burns. sunt qui takes the subjunctive possint — “there are the sort who could believe” — which makes the believers a class rather than named people. The son of Jupiter closes his speech by doubting that there are any gods; the em dash is the editor's, marking where the thought snaps.

sentences.t:
Dixit, perque altam saucius Oeten
haud aliter graditur, quam si venabula taurus
corpore fixa gerat, factique refugerit auctor.
sentences.l: He spoke, and, wounded, paces over high Oeta not otherwise than as if a bull were carrying hunting-spears fixed in his body, and the author of the deed had fled.
sentences.i: So he spoke; and wounded he paces over high Oeta just as a bull might, with hunting-spears standing in his body and the man who threw them run away.
sentences.n: graditur is deponent — passive in form, active in meaning: “he strides”. haud aliter … quam si sets up a comparison that is not being claimed as fact, so its verbs go into the subjunctive (gerat, refugerit). facti auctor is “the maker of the deed”, and his flight is the sharp end of the simile: the bull has the spears in him and nobody left to turn on. Oeta is the mountain in Trachis, and the part stays on that mountain until Hercules is carried off it at the end.

sentences.t:
Saepe illum gemitus edentem, saepe frementem,
saepe retemptantem totas infringere vestes
sternentemque trabes irascentemque videres
montibus aut patrio tendentem bracchia caelo.
sentences.l: Often you might have seen him giving out groans, often roaring, often trying again to tear the whole garment apart, and laying low tree-trunks, and raging at the mountains, or stretching his arms toward his father's sky.
sentences.i: Again and again you might have seen him groaning, roaring, wrenching at the robe to tear the whole of it away, felling tree-trunks, raging at the mountains, or reaching his arms toward the sky that was his father's.
sentences.n: videres is imperfect subjunctive used as a potential of the past, “you might have seen” — a generalising second person that puts the reader on the mountain without naming anyone. A run of accusative participles piles up behind three saepes before videres arrives at the end of the third line and finally gives them a verb, with one more participle following after it. irascentem takes the dative montibus. The arms lifted to his father's sky repeat the gesture of line 175, tollens ad sidera palmas, and get the same answer.

sentences.t:
Ecce Lichan trepidum latitantem rupe cavata
adspicit, utque dolor rabiem conlegerat omnem,
sentences.l: Look — he catches sight of Lichas, trembling, hiding in a hollowed rock; and since his pain had gathered up all its rage,
sentences.i: Then he catches sight of Lichas, shaking, hidden in a hollow of the rock; and because the pain had gathered all its fury,
sentences.n: Ecce is the narrator's “look”, and it turns the poem from the general picture of suffering to one man in one place. Lichan is the Greek form of the accusative of Lichas. rupe cavata is a plain ablative of place, “in a hollowed rock”. ut with the pluperfect indicative conlegerat is temporal here and causal in effect — the rage had already collected, and what follows is what it did.

sentences.t:
“tune, Licha,” dixit “feralia dona dedisti?
Tune meae necis auctor eris?”
sentences.l: “Was it you, Lichas,” he said, “who gave the deadly gifts? Will you be the author of my death?”
sentences.i: “Was it you, Lichas,” he said, “who brought those gifts of death? Will you prove to be the author of my killing?”
sentences.n: Licha is the Greek form of the vocative of Lichas. feralis belongs to funerals and the dead, so feralia dona are gifts fit for a burial. auctor is the same word used of the spear-thrower at line 206: there the maker of the deed had run away, and here Hercules has found one he can reach. nex is a violent death, a killing, not death in general.

sentences.t:
Tremit ille pavetque
pallidus et timide verba excusantia dicit.
sentences.l: He trembles and is afraid, pale, and timidly speaks words of excuse.
sentences.i: He shakes and cowers, white with fear, and timidly gets out words of excuse.
sentences.n: Three verbs and two more markers of fright (pallidus, timide) are spent on him in a line and a half. verba excusantia is “excusing words”, and the poem never says what they were — only that he was making them when he was picked up. Whether the excuse was good is left standing open.

sentences.t:
Dicentem genibusque manus adhibere parantem
corripit Alcides et terque quaterque rotatum
mittit in Euboicas tormento fortius undas.
sentences.l: Him, still speaking and making ready to put his hands to his knees, Alcides snatches up, and, whirled three times and four, hurls him into the Euboean waves more forcibly than a catapult.
sentences.i: Alcides snatches him up as he is still speaking, still reaching to clasp his knees, whirls him three times and four, and slings him into the Euboean sea harder than a catapult could.
sentences.n: genibus manus adhibere is the formal act of supplication — you take hold of the knees of the person you are begging — and he is killed in the middle of doing it. Dicentem and parantem are accusatives hanging in the air until corripit arrives to govern them. terque quaterque, “three times and four”, is a set phrase for “over and over” rather than a count. Alcides names Hercules by his grandfather Alceus; tormentum is the torsion catapult, so the comparison is to a piece of artillery.

sentences.t: Ille per aerias pendens induruit auras,
sentences.l: He, hanging through the airy breezes, grew hard,
sentences.i: As he hung in the air, he hardened,
sentences.n: induruit is an inchoative perfect: he became hard, rather than was hard. The change begins in mid-flight, before he has landed on anything — pendens keeps him suspended while it happens.

sentences.t:
utque ferunt imbres gelidis concrescere ventis,
inde nives fieri, nivibus quoque molle rotatis
adstringi et spissa glomerari grandine corpus:
sentences.l: and as they say that rains thicken in chill winds, that snows are made from them, and that, with the snows whirled about, the soft substance is bound tight and rolled up into packed hail:
sentences.i: and just as they say rain thickens in cold winds, and snow is formed out of it, and snow in its turn, whirled about, has its soft stuff bound tight and packed into hail:
sentences.n: ferunt, “they say”, hands the whole physics lesson to somebody else, and it governs the chain of accusative-and-infinitive that follows (concrescere, fieri, adstringi, glomerari). nivibus rotatis is an ablative absolute inside that chain. quoque here is the plain adverb “too”, not quo plus -que — worth checking each time, because it can be either. molle goes with corpus at the end of the following line, so the adjective and its noun sit a line apart.

sentences.t:
sic illum validis iactum per inane lacertis
exsanguemque metu nec quicquam umoris habentem
in rigidos versum silices prior edidit aetas.
sentences.l: so an earlier age gave out that he — flung through the void by strong arms, drained of blood by fear and holding not a drop of moisture — was turned into hard flint.
sentences.i: so an earlier age handed down that he, flung through the empty air by those strong arms, bloodless with terror and with no moisture left in him, was turned to stiff flint.
sentences.n: prior aetas edidit governs the whole thing as an accusative-and-infinitive, illum … versum (esse): Ovid attributes the change to an older tradition instead of vouching for it, exactly as ferunt did in the simile just above. The comparison is meant physically — whirling drives the water out of snow and leaves hail, and whirling and terror leave Lichas dry, and dry is what stone is. nec quicquam umoris takes a partitive genitive, “not anything of moisture”. inane is the void, empty space.

sentences.t:
Nunc quoque in Euboico scopulus brevis eminet alto
gurgite et humanae servat vestigia formae;
sentences.l: Now too a low rock stands out in the deep Euboean swell and keeps the traces of a human shape;
sentences.i: Even now a low rock juts from the deep Euboean water and keeps the marks of a human form;
sentences.n: Nunc quoque steps out of the story into the reader's own present and points at something still there to be seen. brevis of a rock is “low”, not “short”. servat vestigia formae is the residue the change leaves behind — enough shape left that you can tell what it was, which is what makes the tale checkable at all. quoque is again the adverb.

sentences.t:
quem, quasi sensurum, nautae calcare verentur
appellantque Lichan.—
sentences.l: and this the sailors are afraid to tread on, as though it would feel it, and they call it Lichas.
sentences.i: and sailors will not set foot on it, as though it could still feel, and they call it Lichas.
sentences.n: quasi sensurum is a future participle agreeing with quem: “as though about to feel”. The fear is not that the stone is holy but that the man is still inside it. verentur is deponent — passive in form, active in meaning. appellant Lichan closes the episode the way these tales usually close: the name outlives the man and is fixed to the thing.

sentences.t:
At tu, Iovis inclita proles,
arboribus caesis, quas ardua gesserat Oete,
inque pyram structis, arcum pharetramque capacem
regnaque visuras iterum Troiana sagittas
ferre iubes Poeante satum.
sentences.l: But you, famed offspring of Jupiter, with the trees felled that steep Oeta had borne, and built up into a pyre, bid the son of Poeas carry your bow and your ample quiver and the arrows that were going to see the realms of Troy a second time.
sentences.i: But you, glorious child of Jupiter — the trees that tall Oeta had grown now felled and piled into a pyre — you bid the son of Poeas take up your bow, your deep quiver, and the arrows that were to see Troy a second time.
sentences.n: The poem turns and speaks to Hercules himself: an apostrophe, and it holds the second person through iubes, sternis and recumbis. Two ablative absolutes are chained on the one noun — arboribus caesis … inque pyram structis, the trees felled and then built up. Poeante satum, “the one begotten of Poeas”, names Philoctetes by his father instead of by name. visuras is a future participle, “going to see”, and iterum says the arrows have been to Troy once already, in the hands of the man giving them away.

sentences.t:
Quo flamma ministro est
subdita; dumque avidis comprenditur ignibus agger,
congeriem silvae Nemeaeo vellere summam
sternis et inposita clavae cervice recumbis,
sentences.l: With him as the agent the flame was set beneath; and while the heap catches in greedy fires, you spread the top of the pile of wood with the Nemean fleece, and, with your neck placed upon your club, you lie back,
sentences.i: It was by his hand that the flame was set underneath; and while the pile catches in the hungry fire, you spread the Nemean lion-skin over the top of the wood and lie back, your neck resting on your club,
sentences.n: Quo ministro is an ablative absolute made of two nouns with no participle at all, “with him as the servant” — the way Latin says who did it without giving him a verb. inposita clavae cervice, three lines on, is a second ablative absolute. The Nemean fleece is the skin of the lion crushed at 197. avidis ignibus answers avidae flammae at 172: the same greed, now in a fire he built himself.

sentences.t:
haud alio vultu, quam si conviva iaceres
inter plena meri redimitus pocula sertis.
sentences.l: with no other face than if you were lying as a dinner-guest, wreathed with garlands, among cups full of unmixed wine.
sentences.i: with no different a look on you than if you were reclining at table as a guest, garlanded, among cups brimming with strong wine.
sentences.n: haud alio … quam si with the imperfect subjunctive iaceres makes an unreal comparison, the second in the part after the bull at 205. merum is wine taken neat, without the water Romans ordinarily mixed into it, so these are a hard drinker's cups. The couch, the garland and the full cups are the furniture of a dinner, set down on a pyre; iaceres serves both, since it is the word for reclining at table and for lying dead.

sentences.t:
Iamque valens et in omne latus diffusa sonabat
securosque artus contemptoremque petebat
flamma suum; timuere dei pro vindice terrae.
sentences.l: And now, strong and spread over every side, the flame was roaring and was making for the untroubled limbs and for its own despiser; the gods were afraid for the earth's champion.
sentences.i: And now the fire, strong and spread on every side, roared, and reached for those untroubled limbs and for the man who despised it; the gods were afraid for the earth's champion.
sentences.n: flamma is held back to the first word of the third line, after both its verbs (sonabat, petebat) and both its objects — the noise and the reaching arrive before the thing doing them. securus is “free from care”, so the limbs the fire reaches for are limbs untroubled by it; contemptorem suum splits across the line-end, “its own despiser”. timuere is timuerunt, the -ere perfect again (potuere at 191). vindex terrae is the earth's champion, the one who took its monsters off it.

sentences.t:
Quos ita (sensit enim) laeto Saturnius ore
Iuppiter adloquitur:
sentences.l: And them — for he had noticed — Saturn's son Jupiter addresses thus, with a glad face:
sentences.i: And Jupiter, Saturn's son, having noticed it, speaks to them like this, and his face is glad:
sentences.n: Quos is a connecting relative: a relative pronoun standing where English wants “and them”, which is how Latin ties one sentence to the last. adloquitur is deponent — passive in form, active in meaning. Saturnius answers Saturnia at 176, the name Hercules threw at Juno: the same father, the opposite temper. The parenthesis (sensit enim) explains the glad face before anyone can wonder at it.

sentences.t:
“Nostra est timor iste voluptas,
o superi,
sentences.l: “That fear of yours is our pleasure, gods above,
sentences.i: “Your fear there is a delight to me, gods above,
sentences.n: iste is the demonstrative of the second person, “that … of yours”: the fear belongs to the ones he is talking to. Nostra is the plural for “my”, the same usage Hercules had at 176. superi is literally “the ones above”, the gods of the sky. The subject is timor iste; nostra … voluptas is the predicate, split so that it stands on either side of the fear it describes, and the sentence lands on voluptas.

sentences.t:
totoque libens mihi pectore grator,
quod memoris populi dicor rectorque paterque,
et mea progenies vestro quoque tuta favore est.
sentences.l: and gladly, with my whole heart, I give myself joy that I am called both ruler and father of a people that remembers, and that my offspring too is safe in your goodwill.
sentences.i: and with my whole heart I gladly count myself fortunate that I am called ruler and father of a people that does not forget, and that my own child is safe in your goodwill too.
sentences.n: grator is deponent — passive in form, active in meaning — and takes the dative mihi: “I give myself joy”. dicor is a true passive with two predicate nominatives hung on it, rector and pater, so “I am called X and Y”; the -que … -que doubling is an epic mannerism. memoris populi is “of a people that remembers”, and memor is the word for gratitude that has not forgotten; from the context that people is the gods he is addressing, who have just proved their memory by being afraid, though the word would serve for humankind as well.

sentences.t:
Nam quamquam ipsius datis hoc inmanibus actis,
obligor ipse tamen.
sentences.l: For although you give this to his own prodigious deeds, still I myself am put under obligation.
sentences.i: For though it is his own monstrous deeds you are honouring, it is I who am left in your debt.
sentences.n: datis is second person plural, “you give”: Jupiter concedes that their alarm is owed to what Hercules did rather than to whose son he is, and then claims the debt anyway. obligor, “I am bound”, is the language of an obligation incurred, and ipse … ipse sets his own person against Hercules' own deeds. inmanis is monstrous in size rather than in wickedness. Magnus prints datis; some editions print datur, “this is given”, which drops the gods out of the clause and leaves the giving unattributed.

sentences.t:
Sed enim ne pectora vano
fida metu paveant: Oetaeas spernite flammas!
sentences.l: But indeed, so that your loyal hearts may not quake with an empty fear — scorn the flames of Oeta!
sentences.i: But so that loyal hearts of yours need not quake at a groundless fear: think nothing of the flames on Oeta!
sentences.n: ne … paveant is a negative purpose clause that looks forward to the command it is attached to; the colon is the editor's way of showing where the two join. Magnus prints ne; some editions print nec, which would make the clause a wish standing on its own, “and let not your loyal hearts quake”, instead of a purpose looking forward to the order. fida pectora is a compliment paid to them in passing, mid-sentence. spernite is the plural imperative, “despise them”, and it answers contemptorem at 240: the fire has one man who despises it and is now to have a heaven full.

sentences.t:
Omnia qui vicit, vincet, quos cernitis, ignes
nec nisi materna Vulcanum parte potentem
sentiet:
sentences.l: He who has conquered all things will conquer the fires you look at, and will feel Vulcan strong only in the part that is his mother's:
sentences.i: The man who has conquered everything will conquer these fires you are watching, and will feel the fire-god's power only in the part he has from his mother:
sentences.n: vicit and vincet stand in the same line, perfect against future: what he has already done and what he will do to this. quos cernitis is folded in between vincet and its object ignes, so the fires are interrupted by their own relative clause. Vulcanum is the god's name used for the fire itself — a metonymy so ordinary that “to feel Vulcan” simply means to be burnt. materna parte is the half of him that came from Alcmena, and it is the only half that can be reached.

sentences.t:
aeternum est a me quod traxit et expers
atque inmune necis nullaque domabile flamma.
sentences.l: what he drew from me is everlasting, and has no share in death and is exempt from it, and is tameable by no flame.
sentences.i: what he drew from me is everlasting: it has no part in death, no liability to it, and no flame can tame it.
sentences.n: expers and inmune both live off the one genitive necis — Latin lets a single case-form serve two adjectives that would each want their own in English. domabile is an adjective in -bilis, “capable of being tamed”, with its agent in the bare ablative nulla flamma. traxit, “drew”, is the verb for taking a quality from a parent, and what he drew from Jupiter is what the fire cannot touch.

sentences.t:
Idque ego defunctum terra caelestibus oris
accipiam, cunctisque meum laetabile factum
dis fore confido.
sentences.l: And that part, once it is done with earth, I shall receive on the shores of heaven, and I trust that my deed will be a gladness to all the gods.
sentences.i: And when it has finished with earth I shall take it in on the shores of heaven; and I trust my act will be a joy to every god.
sentences.n: defungor is deponent — active in meaning though passive in form — and takes an ablative of the thing one is finished with, so defunctum terra is “having discharged earth”, done with it. oris is from ora, a coast: heaven is given a shoreline to be received on. fore is the older future infinitive of sum, standing for futurum esse, and it depends on confido.

sentences.t:
Siquis tamen Hercule, siquis
forte deo doliturus erit, data praemia nolet,
sed meruisse dari sciet invitusque probabit.”
sentences.l: If anyone, however, shall grieve at Hercules — at Hercules a god — that one will not want the rewards given, but will know that they deserved to be given, and unwilling he will approve.”
sentences.i: If anyone, though, is going to be pained at Hercules — at Hercules made a god — that one will not want the honours granted, but will know they were earned, and will approve them against his will.”
sentences.n: doliturus erit is a future participle with erit, the periphrastic way of saying “is going to grieve”. The repeated siquis makes the point twice, and the second time adds deo: it is not Hercules that will hurt, it is Hercules turned god. meruisse dari puts a passive infinitive under a perfect one, “to have deserved to be given”. invitusque probabit is a contradiction of will held in two words, approval got out of unwillingness — and the person meant is left unnamed.

sentences.t:
Adsensere dei: coniunx quoque regia visa est
cetera non duro, duro tamen ultima vultu
dicta tulisse Iovis seque indoluisse notatam.
sentences.l: The gods assented; the royal wife too seemed to have borne the rest of Jupiter's words with a face not hard, yet the last of them with a hard one, and to have grieved at being marked out.
sentences.i: The gods assented; and Jupiter's royal wife too was seen to take the rest of his words with a face not hard — the last of them with a hard one — and to smart at being singled out.
sentences.n: visa est is the personal passive of video, so what hangs on it is nominative-and-infinitive: coniunx is the nominative subject and seemed to have borne and to have grieved, where English wants “it seemed that she…”. Inside that, se … notatam is a further accusative-and-infinitive under indoluisse. non duro, duro — the same adjective denied and then granted, on either side of the pause — is the whole sentence compressed into one repeated adjective: she was calm until the last thing he said. notatam is the word for being publicly marked or pointed at; he never named her, and she knew who was meant. Adsensere is adsenserunt, the -ere perfect a third time (potuere 191, timuere 241).

sentences.l: Meanwhile whatever there was that the flame could ravage Mulciber had taken away, and there remained no likeness of Hercules to be recognised;
sentences.i: Meanwhile the fire-god had carried off whatever the flame could destroy, and no shape of Hercules was left to be recognised;
sentences.n: Mulciber, “the softener”, is another name for Vulcan and another way of saying fire — the second such substitution in a dozen lines, after Vulcanum at 251. populabile has its agent in the dative flammae, where domabile at 253 had the same relation in the ablative (nulla flamma) — verse uses either; cognoscenda is a gerundive doing the same work in the negative, “not to be recognised”. effigies is the look of a thing rather than the thing: what burnt away was the appearance of him.

sentences.t:
nec quicquam ab imagine ductum
matris habet, tantumque Iovis vestigia servat.
sentences.l: nor does he keep anything drawn from his mother's likeness, and he preserves the traces of Jupiter only.
sentences.i: nor does he keep anything taken from his mother's likeness; only the traces of Jupiter are left in him.
sentences.n: vestigia servat is the same phrase used of the rock at 227 — that stone keeps the traces of a human shape, and this man keeps the traces of a god. The tense shifts here from abstulerat and remansit to the present habet and servat: the burning is finished, and what he is now is stated in the present. ductum, “drawn”, is the word for taking a copy off an original.

sentences.t:
Utque novus serpens posita cum pelle senecta
luxuriare solet squamaque nitere recenti,
sentences.l: And as a snake, made new with its old age shed along with its skin, is accustomed to run riot and to shine with a fresh scale,
sentences.i: And as a snake, made new when it has sloughed its old age off along with its skin, will grow lush and glisten with fresh scales,
sentences.n: posita cum pelle senecta is an ablative absolute in which senecta, the old age, is the thing put off and the skin merely comes with it — which is the point of the comparison. luxuriare is normally said of plants running to growth, so the new body is treated as an overflow rather than a repair. This is the last of the part's four extended comparisons (the bull at 205, the hail at 220, the dinner-guest at 237).

sentences.t:
sic, ubi mortales Tirynthius exuit artus,
parte sui meliore viget maiorque videri
coepit et augusta fieri gravitate verendus.
sentences.l: so, when the Tirynthian had put off his mortal limbs, he flourishes in the better part of himself, and began to seem greater and to become one to be revered, in august dignity.
sentences.i: so, once the Tirynthian had shed his mortal limbs, he thrives in the better part of himself; and he began to look larger and to grow awesome in a stately weight of presence.
sentences.n: exuit is the verb for stripping off clothing, so the mortal limbs come away like the snake's skin — the simile and the thing compared share a word. viget is present and coepit is perfect in the same sentence: the flourishing is a standing state, the growing was a moment. videri is the passive infinitive of video, “to be seen” and so “to seem”. verendus is a gerundive used as a plain adjective, “one who must be revered”. parte sui meliore names what survived — the part drawn from Jupiter at 252. Tirynthius calls Hercules by Tiryns, the city he was reared in.

sentences.t:
Quem pater omnipotens inter cava nubila raptum
quadriiugo curru radiantibus intulit astris.
sentences.l: And him, snatched up amid the hollow clouds, the almighty father brought in a four-horse chariot to the radiant stars.
sentences.i: And the almighty father caught him up through the hollow clouds and carried him in a four-horse chariot to the shining stars.
sentences.n: Quem is a connecting relative again — Latin's way of opening a sentence with “and him”. cava nubila makes the cloud a hollow thing to be carried through rather than a surface. intulit takes the dative radiantibus astris: he is brought in among the stars, and the part ends on that arrival and says nothing further. quadriiugo is “four-yoked”, the chariot word.
